text:
Short answer: no. The all-male panel isn't evidence of anything in your case, and leading with it would hurt you.

**Why it doesn't work as a signal**

A sex discrimination argument needs the panel's composition to connect to a disadvantage you suffered because of your sex. You're a man, and the person who got the job is a man. Whatever the panel did, it didn't disfavour male candidates. If anything, a homogeneous panel's affinity biases would have run toward you as much as toward him.

An all-male selection panel is a legitimate thing to criticise in general — it's poor practice, and many consultancies have internal policies requiring mixed panels. But "this panel was badly constituted" and "this panel discriminated against me" are different claims, and only the second one gives you anything. Raising the first in a grievance about your own rejection reads as scraping for ammunition, which undercuts the parts of your complaint that actually have substance.

**What's more likely going on**

The experience gap is real — fifteen years and three major projects against eight years — but it isn't itself evidence of impropriety. Head of group is not the same job as senior designer. A substantial part of it is winning and keeping work, managing client expectations, and being the face of the group. "Excellent client relationships" is a legitimate and quite possibly decisive criterion for that role, and a panel is entitled to weigh it above raw design years. That's a judgement call you can disagree with, not a defect.

Worth sitting with honestly: is that where you were weaker? If your fifteen years are heavily design- and delivery-weighted and his eight include a lot of client-facing and business development work, the panel may have made a defensible call. Two interviews and a final three means you were taken seriously.

**The one thread with any coherence**

If there's a protected characteristic in play at all, it's age, not sex — you're in your forties, he presumably isn't, and you lost despite nearly double the experience. But that's thin on its own. Being older and more experienced and not getting a job is not evidence of age discrimination; you'd need something more, like age-related remarks in the interviews, a pattern in recent appointments, or a stated rationale that's a proxy for age. "Client relationships" isn't one. I'd keep this in the back of your mind rather than put it in writing now.

**What to actually do**

The unanswered request is your real issue, though two weeks of silence is more likely disorganisation than stonewalling.

1. Send a short, neutral follow-up to whoever you asked, referencing the date of the original request and asking for feedback against the published selection criteria. Frame it as developmental — you want to know what to strengthen for the next opportunity. You'll get far more out of them that way than with a complaint framing.
2. Note that in most jurisdictions there's no legal right to written reasons for a hiring decision. So ask well rather than demand.
3. If you genuinely suspect the process was improper, a data subject access request will get you the interview notes and scoring that relate to you personally. That's a serious step that changes the relationship, so don't take it unless you mean it.
4. Separately, if your employer has a mixed-panel policy that wasn't followed, that's a fair process observation to raise — but raise it on its own terms, later, not bundled into this.

The strongest version of your position is: fifteen years, three major projects, final three, two interviews, and no feedback after a fortnight. That's a reasonable person asking a reasonable question. Adding the panel composition makes it weaker, not stronger.
